blocks.text: Config management tools converge servers toward a declared state; golden images bake a pre-configured OS image. Both fought drift before containers, with different trade-offs.

rows: Puppet, Chef (agent, pull), Salt, Ansible (agentless, push over SSH)
Describe desired state; apply idempotently to running servers
Convergence is slow; drift between runs; manual changes still possible; ordering and partial failures
Bake a full machine image once, launch many
GB-sized, slow to rebuild; OS + app coupled; image sprawl
Bake only the app's userland; run on any host
Shared kernel; state must live elsewhere

blocks.text: Applying the same playbook twice yields the same state, e.g. "ensure package X version Y is installed". That's declarative configuration, which containers push further by baking the result at build time instead of converging at runtime.
Why they didn't make containers unnecessary

items: They manage machines, not applications as portable artifacts.
Runtime convergence can fail halfway; image builds either succeed or produce nothing.
They're still used to provision the hosts that run containers (and for non-container infra).

blocks.text: Q: "How do Ansible/Puppet differ from Docker images?" A: "Config management converges live servers toward a declared state at runtime and can leave them partially converged or drifted; a Docker image is built once, immutable, and run identically anywhere. Today config management often provisions the hosts while images package the apps."

items: Golden images = baked machine images, heavy.
Containers bake just the app, immutably.
The tools complement each other: hosts vs apps.
